docs.title: Smart Factory Dashboard
docs.summary: How I used Claude Design, Claude Chat, and Claude Code together to go from a design system prompt to a fully working smart factory dashboard — no Figma, no handoff friction.

chunks.text:
From design system prompt → Claude Design → Claude Code → live demo
  

I wanted to see how far I could push the new Claude toolchain — Claude Chat, Claude Design, and Claude Code — as an end-to-end product design and engineering workflow. No Figma. No separate handoff. Just prompts, a design system, and code.

The result: a fully working Smart Factory OS dashboard for display panel manufacturing (OLED/LCD), with an interactive process map, AI agent workflow panel, and a Notion-style schedule calendar.

You can see the live demo here: factory-dashboard-demo

Here's exactly how I built it, step by step.

The idea

Modern semiconductor and display fabs run on MES (Manufacturing Execution Systems) — dense, often ugly enterprise software. I wanted to explore what a premium, calm, SaaS-quality factory control interface could look like if you designed it the way you'd design a great B2B product.

The concept: FabOS — a smart factory intelligence platform for display panel production. Three panels, one canvas:

- A central interactive process map (glass substrate → cleaning → deposition → lithography → inspection → cell assembly → QC)
- A left AI agent / workflow panel with draggable job cards
- A right Notion-style schedule calendar for orchestrating agent runs

The visual inspiration came from aircraft freight dashboards and clean-room control panels — light gray backgrounds, rounded cards, pill tabs, minimal black accents. Industrial, but calm.

Step 1 — Building the design system in Claude Chat

Before touching Claude Design, I used Claude Chat to define the design system itself. I shared three reference images — an air freight logistics dashboard, a BIM construction tool, and a dark data card — and wrote a detailed concept prompt describing the factory dashboard vision.

Claude generated a full design system reference — color palette, typography scale, status language, spacing tokens, and mood board — rendered as an interactive widget right in the chat.

📐 Design System Reference (click to expand)

The key decisions that came out of this step:

FabOS Design Tokens

300/400/500/600 — all UI, headings, labels

#7C3AED — Reserved for AI agents and orchestration
          

Forbidden

❌ Dark backgrounds

❌ Gradients

❌ Neon effects

Required

          Mood: Clean Room Precision — like aircraft avionics, zero noise, total operational clarity.
        

Step 2 — Setting up the design system in Claude Design

With the system defined, I opened Claude Design and filled in the Design System tab.

Company name / Design system name:

Notes field (this persists across every generation in the tab):

Once the notes field is set, Claude Design already understands the visual language before I write a single generation prompt. Every component it produces automatically inherits the fonts, colors, and spacing rules.

Step 3 — Generating the dashboard design

With the design system loaded, I prompted Claude Design to generate the three-panel dashboard layout. The key to a good result was being specific about each panel's behavior, not just its appearance.

The prompt described:

A few minutes later, Claude Design produced a high-fidelity mockup that faithfully reflected the FabOS design language — pill navigation, off-white background, rounded process modules in the center, violet-accented agent cards on the left, clean calendar event blocks on the right.

The iteration cycle here was genuinely fast. When a component didn't look right — say, the calendar grid was too dense — I described the change in plain language ("make the time slots taller, reduce grid line weight, soften the event block typography") and got an updated version in seconds.

Step 4 — Iterating on components

A few specific components needed extra passes.

Process map modules — The first version rendered process steps as simple labeled boxes. I pushed for more: each module needed a status indicator dot, a WIP lot count badge, and a subtle selection highlight state. After two iterations the modules felt like real equipment cells — selectable, scannable, information-dense without being cluttered.

AI agent cards — Getting the violet accent right took a couple of tries. The goal was that violet cards should feel distinctly different from regular workflow cards without breaking the overall light palette. The solution was a soft #EDE9FE background with #7C3AED text and a violet left-border accent — unmistakably AI, but still calm.

Schedule calendar — The hardest panel to get right. Early versions looked like a Gantt chart. The fix was removing most of the grid lines, increasing vertical padding on time slots, and treating each scheduled workflow as a rounded card rather than a bar — much closer to how Notion Calendar handles events.

Step 5 — Sharing to Claude Code

Once the design was solid, I used Claude Design's Share to Claude Code function. It exports the design context — component structure, spacing, color values, font choices — directly into a Claude Code session.

The implementation prompt was straightforward — just Copy Command and paste into the Claude Code CLI:

Claude Design temporarily hosts the design file, and Claude Code fetches and implements it.

Claude Code scaffolded the component structure and wired up interactive state — selected module, detail panel view, calendar view toggle — and applied the design tokens directly from the exported context. The color variables, border radii, and font weights all carried over more cleanly than I expected.

The drag-and-drop from the agent panel onto the calendar required a bit of extra prompting to nail the UX. Once I described the interaction precisely, Claude Code handled the underlying logic well. For example:

When the desired behavior is described concretely, Claude Code wires up the matching state management and event handling on its own.

What the final dashboard looks like

The live demo at factory-dashboard-demo shows the full three-panel layout in action. Even the GitHub Pages deploy was a single Claude Code command.

- Center (process map) — Display panel production flow from glass substrate input through final QC. Each process module is clickable, surfacing WIP count, equipment status, and active alarms.
- Left (AI agent panel) — Agent and workflow cards. Violet accents mark agent-driven actions; blues mark standard workflows.
- Right (Schedule) — A Notion-style calendar. Scheduled runs render as clean event blocks, color-coded by workflow category.

The interface ends up feeling like the original aircraft freight dashboard inspiration applied to factory operations — light, calm, technical, trustworthy.

What worked well

The design system notes field is the real unlock. Once it's set up correctly, every subsequent generation starts from the right place. You don't re-explain fonts and colors every time — Claude already knows.

Claude Design → Claude Code handoff is surprisingly tight. The exported design context carries enough information that Claude Code doesn't have to guess at colors or spacing. The gap between "this is what it should look like" and "this is the code" is much smaller than a traditional Figma-to-developer handoff.

Specificity beats verbosity. Long prompts describing the general vibe produce mediocre results. Short, precise prompts describing specific interactions ("clicking a process module shows a slide-in detail panel with lot status, active recipe, and assigned agent") produce good ones.

What I'd do differently

The process map is still more illustrative than truly data-driven. In a real implementation you'd want the process module states (running, alarm, idle) driven by live WebSocket data from the MES backend. That's a Claude Code conversation for another day.

The drag-and-drop scheduling also has edge cases — overlapping events, multi-day workflows — that would need more careful product thinking before shipping to actual factory operators.

The workflow, summarized

Total time from first prompt to working demo: roughly half a day.

The toolchain is genuinely useful for this kind of work — complex, data-rich B2B interfaces where the design language needs to be precise and component interactions need to be carefully specified. The Claude Chat → Claude Design → Claude Code pipeline removes most of the translation friction that usually lives between design and engineering. The $110 I spent on Claude is a separate matter.

If you're building MES dashboards, logistics control panels, or any operations-centric SaaS, the approach above is a solid starting point.

docs.title: KMeans Clustering
docs.summary: A from-scratch KMeans clustering visualizer — four init methods, step-by-step Lloyd's iterations — rebuilt as a stateless JSON API and embedded as a live, interactive demo right in the post.

chunks.text:
Clustering asks a simple question of unlabeled data: which points belong together?
KMeans is the classic first answer. You give it the number of groups you want — k — and
it splits the points into k clusters, each gathered around its own center, or centroid.
There are no labels and no training signal; it works purely from how close the points are to
one another.

The algorithm is short enough to keep in your head: drop k centroids, assign every point to
its nearest one, move each centroid to the mean of the points it captured, and repeat until
nothing moves. That loop is Lloyd's algorithm — and the fastest way to understand it is to
watch it run. Pick a dataset and an init method, then Step through the iterations or Run
to convergence; in manual mode, click the canvas to drop your k centroids first.

Lloyd's iteration algorithm

KMeans repeats two steps until nothing moves. Write  for each data point and  for
each cluster's center, its centroid. The first step — assign — assigns every point to its
nearest centroid: point 's cluster label  is whichever centroid index j makes the
squared distance  smallest — that's all  means, "the
j that minimizes it":

then update moves each centroid to the mean of the points now assigned to it. Writing
 for the set of points now assigned to cluster j and  for how many there are, the
centroid becomes their average position:

Why those two steps in particular? Because each one chips away at the same quantity — the
within-cluster sum of squares, written . For every cluster j, add up the squared
distance from each of its points  to that cluster's centroid , then sum over all k
clusters:

Assign lowers  with the centroids fixed; update lowers  with the assignments
fixed. Neither step can ever raise , and there are only finitely many ways to split the
points into clusters — so the cost can't keep falling forever. It drops until a full pass
changes nothing, then stops. That's why it always converges. (Watch the cost in the demo
tick down and flatten out.)

But where it lands depends entirely on where the centroids start: KMeans only ever walks
downhill, so a bad start settles into a bad local minimum. That's the interesting part — and
why the next section is about initialization.

Four ways to start

Lloyd's algorithm only ever walks downhill, so the starting centroids decide which local minimum
you settle into — initialization is the single biggest lever on the result. There are many ways to
seed it; here are four of the most common:

- Random. Pick k of the actual data points at random and call them the starting
  centroids. The catch is variance:
  every run can land differently, and an unlucky draw (two seeds inside the same true cluster)
  leaves a centroid with nothing to claim, so it splits a real cluster in half. The usual fix is
  brute force — re-run with fresh seeds and keep the lowest-cost result.
- Farthest First. Pick the first centroid at random, then each next one is the point
  farthest from every centroid chosen so far. After a few picks the seeds are spread across the
  whole space — exactly what Random can't guarantee. The downside: the farthest point is almost
  always an outlier, so this reliably spends a centroid on a lone speck of noise out at the
  edge.
- KMeans++. The probabilistic middle ground, and the one to actually use. The first centroid
  is random; each next one is drawn with probability proportional to its squared distance to
  the nearest already-chosen centroid (, where  is that
  nearest-centroid distance). Faraway points are far likelier to be picked, so the seeds spread
  out — but because it's a draw and not a hard maximum, a single outlier no longer hijacks a
  centroid. It's scikit-learn's default and comes with a guarantee that the expected cost is
  within  of optimal.
- Manual. Place the k centroids yourself. Less a strategy than the teaching mode: pile all
  the seeds into one corner and watch the run crawl outward, or drop one inside each visible blob
  and watch it lock on in a single step — the fastest way to feel how much the start decides the
  finish.

Where KMeans breaks

Good initialization cures bad luck — but two failure modes are baked into the algorithm
itself, and no amount of restarting fixes them. Switch the dataset above to see each one:

- Clusters of very different sizes. Pick Uneven blobs: the big, loosely spread cluster
  gets carved up, because its outer points sit closer to a neighboring centroid than to their
  own. KMeans balances distances, not membership, so it splits the large cluster to "help"
  the small ones.
- Non-globular shapes. KMeans assumes every cluster is a round blob sitting around its mean.
  Pick Two moons and set k = 2: you read the two interlocking crescents instantly, but
  each point just goes to the nearest centroid, so KMeans can only draw a straight boundary — it
  slices across both moons instead of following them.

These aren't bugs you can re-run away; they're the price of assuming round, comparably sized
clusters. When your data looks like that, KMeans is hard to beat. When it doesn't, you reach for
something else — DBSCAN, spectral clustering, Gaussian mixtures.

Assign, update, repeat

That really is the whole algorithm. KMeans isn't the sharpest clustering method, but it's the one
you can hold entirely in your head — and the one whose every move you just watched land on the
canvas above. Once the loop feels obvious, the failure modes and the seeding tricks stop being
trivia to memorize and turn into things you can see coming. Change the dataset, reseed, and run it
again: it isn't a black box anymore.

docs.title: Quantum Simulator
docs.summary: Implementing the same quantum circuits three ways — Qiskit, a NumPy statevector engine, and Google's TensorNetwork — to actually understand what a quantum gate does under the hood.

chunks.text:
Quantum computing isn't a far-future thing anymore. IBM, Google, and a handful of startups have actual quantum hardware you can run circuits on from the cloud. But the hardware is noisy and slow, and as soon as you go past a few qubits, you really need a classical simulator to develop and verify algorithms.

I wanted to actually understand what those simulators do — not just call circuit.run() and trust the output. So I built the same quantum circuits three different ways: with IBM's Qiskit, with a NumPy-based statevector engine I wrote from scratch, and with Google's TensorNetwork library. Same gates, same algorithms, three completely different implementations underneath.

The result is a small framework + a React/Three.js demo where you can drag gates onto qubits and run the circuit in your browser. You can try the live demo here, and the full source is on GitHub.

Here's what I learned building it.

The idea

Most quantum tutorials show you a single framework — usually Qiskit — and walk you through Bell states and Grover's algorithm. That's great for getting a feel for the API, but it leaves a black box where the simulator should be. What does it actually mean to "apply a Hadamard gate to qubit 0"? Is the simulator multiplying a giant matrix? Storing  amplitudes? Doing something cleverer?

The answer turns out to be yes, all of the above, depending on which simulator you pick. So I built three:

- Qiskit simulator — IBM's framework. Used to implement Grover's algorithm and as the reference output.
- Statevector simulator — Pure NumPy. Stores the full  amplitude vector. Every gate becomes a Kronecker-expanded matrix multiplication. The textbook approach.
- Tensor network simulator — Built on Google's TensorNetwork. Represents the circuit as a graph of small tensors. The full state is never materialized until you contract.

The whole thing is wrapped in a Flask API and a React frontend so you can build a circuit visually and see all three engines produce the same result.

Step 1 — Wrapping Qiskit to build intuition

I started with Qiskit because IBM's tooling makes it easy to draw circuits and see what you're doing. The goal here wasn't to reinvent anything — it was to implement Grover's algorithm as a reference and make sure I understood it well enough to reimplement it from scratch later.

Grover's algorithm is a quantum search algorithm. Given an unstructured list of N items and a way to recognize the right one, classical search takes O(N) operations on average. Grover does it in O(√N). It's not exponential speedup, but it's real and it generalizes.

The algorithm has three parts:

1. Initialization — Apply H to every qubit. Now all  basis states have equal amplitude.
2. Oracle — Flip the sign of the amplitude on the "answer" state.
3. Diffuser — Reflect all amplitudes around the average. The negative one gets amplified.

Repeat Oracle + Diffuser about √N times. Measure. With high probability, you get the answer.

That's the Grover circuit for a 3-qubit search. The left block is initialization, the middle is the oracle, the right is the diffuser. The MCX (multi-controlled X) gates are where most of the work happens — they're how the oracle "recognizes" the marked state.

Implementing this in Qiskit was almost embarrassingly short:

But that's the point — Qiskit hides everything interesting behind .append(). The next two simulators do the opposite.

Step 2 — A statevector simulator in raw NumPy

The statevector approach is the textbook way to simulate a quantum circuit. The state of n qubits is a complex vector of length . Every gate is a unitary matrix. Applying a gate means matrix-multiplying:

The catch is that U has to be the size of the whole system. If you want to apply a Hadamard to qubit 1 of a 3-qubit system, you can't just multiply by the 2×2 Hadamard matrix — you need an 8×8 matrix that acts as Hadamard on qubit 1 and identity on the others. That's where the Kronecker product comes in (with qubit 0 as the leftmost tensor factor):

In NumPy:

That's the whole engine. Wrap it in a StatevectorCircuit class, add convenience methods for each gate, and you have a working simulator:

The controlled gates need slightly more care — a CNOT isn't just kron(CX, I), because the control and target qubits might not be adjacent. You have to construct the right block-diagonal matrix that leaves  on the control alone and flips the target when the control is . Once you've written that helper, every other controlled gate (CZ, CCX, MCX) falls out as a special case.

What the gate matrices actually look like:

A few things worth saying about specific gates, because writing them out by hand really did change how I think about them:

H is the gate that creates superposition. . Apply it to every qubit and you get a uniform superposition over all  basis states. Every quantum algorithm I know of starts here.

Z and S and T look identical when you measure. They only change phases on the  component. But phases matter the moment you put another H after them — that's how interference happens, and interference is the whole reason quantum is faster than classical for some problems.

CNOT is how you make entanglement.  followed by CNOT turns  into the Bell state . Two qubits that are perfectly correlated even though neither has a definite value on its own.

Toffoli (CCX) is universal. Combined with H, you can build any quantum circuit. That's also where you encode classical logic (AND, NAND) into a quantum computer.

The statevector simulator is clear, short, and fast for small systems. The problem shows up around 20–25 qubits, where  complex numbers per state and  entries per gate matrix start to actually hurt your laptop.

Step 3 — A tensor network simulator with Google TensorNetwork

This is the part I was most excited about. Tensor networks are a way of representing high-dimensional tensors as graphs of small ones, and they map onto quantum circuits almost too neatly.

Each node in the picture is a small tensor — a qubit, or a gate. The lines between them are edges, which represent shared tensor indices. Applying a gate to a qubit means inserting a new node and connecting its input edge to the qubit's current output edge. That's it. No giant matrix.

Running the circuit means contracting all the edges — summing over the shared indices until only the open ones remain. The result is the final state vector. The crucial difference from statevector: nothing is ever materialized to its full  size during the build phase. The framework can choose a smart contraction order at the end.

In code:

The API is intentionally identical to the statevector simulator — same method names, same semantics. The difference is entirely in what happens underneath. tn.h([0]) adds a Hadamard tensor node to the network and rewires one edge. It doesn't compute anything. tn.run() is the moment of truth: TensorNetwork walks the graph, picks a contraction order, and produces the final state.

For small circuits, statevector is actually faster — less overhead. But as the circuit gets deeper or wider, the tensor network version starts to win, because it can avoid constructing the giant intermediate matrices that statevector forces on itself.

Step 4 — Wrapping it all in a browser

Three Python engines aren't much fun unless you can actually play with them. So I built a React + react-three-fiber frontend and a Flask backend that exposes all three simulators over a single API.

The frontend lets you pick the number of qubits, drag gates onto a circuit, and run the whole thing. Three.js made the 3D circuit feel less like an enterprise tool and more like something you'd actually want to mess with.

The whole thing is deployed on Railway. You can try the live demo.

Trying a Bell state. The simplest non-trivial circuit: H on qubit 0, then CNOT(0, 1). If everything is wired up correctly, you should see  and  each at ~50% probability, and  /  at zero. Two entangled qubits.

Running Grover on 3 qubits with the marked state . Initialize with H on all qubits, apply the oracle for , then the diffuser. After a single iteration the probability of measuring  should dominate.

What's nice is that you can flip the simulator backend in the UI and confirm all three engines produce the same distribution. They should, of course — they're all simulating the same math — but seeing it line up is the kind of validation you only get from owning the whole stack.

What worked well

Implementing the same gates three ways made them actually click. Reading "H creates superposition" in a textbook is one thing. Writing (1/sqrt(2))  [[1,1],[1,-1]], Kronecker-expanding it to the full system, multiplying it into a state vector, and seeing the amplitudes split — that's when it sticks.

Identical APIs across the three simulators paid off. Same method names, same shapes, same outputs. It let me write the frontend once and treat the choice of engine as just a backend flag. It also made debugging trivial: if statevector and tensornetwork disagreed on a circuit, one of them had a bug.

Tensor networks are surprisingly approachable. I went in expecting the library to be intimidating, but TensorNetwork's API is small. Most of the conceptual weight is in understanding which edges to contract when — and the library handles that for you.

What I'd do differently

The performance comparison deserves a real benchmark. I have a runtimecomparison.py script that runs the same circuit through statevector and tensornetwork at increasing qubit counts, but it's a single-machine, single-run measurement. A proper benchmark — multiple circuit topologies, repeated trials, memory profiling — would tell a much more honest story.

The 3D circuit is fun but not necessarily better. I picked react-three-fiber because I wanted to see what it could do, not because the problem demanded 3D. A clean 2D circuit editor in the Qiskit style would probably be more usable for actual work. I'd keep the 3D as a toggle or an Easter egg.

No noise model. All three simulators are ideal — they assume perfect gates and no decoherence. Real quantum hardware is dominated by noise. Adding a depolarizing channel or a T1/T2 model would make the simulator much closer to what you'd hit on actual IBM hardware.

The takeaway

If you're learning quantum computing and you've been bouncing between Qiskit tutorials without quite feeling like you get it, I'd suggest implementing a statevector simulator yourself. It's about 200 lines of NumPy. By the time you've written the gate matrices and Kronecker-expanded your first CNOT, you'll have a much clearer mental model of what's actually happening than any number of circuit.draw() calls would give you.

And once that clicks, tensor networks are the natural next step — same physics, different representation, much better scaling. Google's library does most of the heavy lifting.

A self-directed studybook working through the fundamentals of graphic design — grid systems,
typographic hierarchy, colour, and the rhythm of a printed page. Each spread takes up a single
principle and then applies it, so the book itself becomes the final design artifact, not just a
record of one.

edge to turn.

docs.title: Jae Hong Lee
docs.summary: Jae Hong Lee (이재홍) is a design engineer based in Seoul. He studied computer science and visual arts, and works at the seam of CS, design, and AI — designing an interface and building what's underneath it, models included. He cares about precision and craft over spectacle.

chunks.heading: Background
chunks.text:
I studied Computer Science at Boston University with a minor in Visual Arts,
including a visiting year in Computer Science & Engineering at Korea University.
My technical background spans algorithm design, AI and machine learning, and
quantum computing; the visual side spans typography, drawing, and motion.

chunks.heading: Work
chunks.text:
I work as a software engineer at LG CNS in Seoul on smart factory systems.
Before that I worked on machine-learning problems at LSAT Lab and LSAT Demon
(time-series deep learning and LLM development), did undergraduate computer
vision research in Boston University's IVC group, and spent two research
internships at the Korea Electronics Technology Institute on quantum computing
and computer vision. I co-authored a publication on machine-learning-based hand
pose generation using a haptic controller.

chunks.heading: How I work
chunks.text:
I like building the whole seam: designing an interface and then building what
runs underneath it, models included. This site is an example — the landing page
embeds your question, retrieves from my own writing, and answers with citations
back to the source. Precision and craft over spectacle.
